# Study Design & Data Ethics {#sec-study-design}

*From the 10/28 in-class activity (Day 9)*

The design of a study decides which conclusions the data can support, before any code is written.

## Study Designs

| Design | What happens | Can show causation? | Watch out for |
|:--------------|:----------------------|:--------------|:------------------|
| **Randomized experiment** | Researcher randomly **assigns** a treatment | Yes, within the sample | Volunteers may not represent everyone; short time frames |
| **Observational, cross-sectional** | Measure people once, at one point in time | No (association) | Confounders; self-report errors |
| **Observational, longitudinal** | Measure the same people repeatedly over time | No, but shows change within people | **Attrition** (people drop out, often not at random) |
| **Observational, retrospective** | Use records that already exist (sales, gym entries) | No | Records weren't made to answer this question |

- **Confounding variable:** a third variable related to both the predictor and the outcome (e.g. screen time could affect both sleep and GPA)
- **Before-and-after** comparisons with no comparison group can't separate the change from everything else that changed (season, prices, marketing)

!! **Random assignment ≠ random sampling**

- Random **assignment** (who gets which treatment) → supports **causal** conclusions
- Random **sampling** (who is in the study) → supports **generalizing** to the population
- An experiment on volunteers at one company shows cause *for those volunteers*, but not necessarily for everyone

## Ways to Collect Data

| Method | Good for | Limitation |
|:----------------|:--------------------------|:---------------------------|
| Survey / self-report | Internal experiences (stress, mood, opinions) | Recall error, social desirability, nonresponse |
| Interviews / focus groups | How people *describe* experiences, in their words | Small samples; stigma can cause underreporting |
| Wearables / tracking | Objective, repeated measures (sleep, steps) | Device errors; only reaches people who own one |
| Naturally generated records | Large volumes of real behavior, cheap | Not designed for research; missing context |
| Web scraping / APIs | Public data at scale (prices, posts, sports stats) | Site terms, changing page layouts; users aren't representative |

A data collection plan should name: target population, data source, collection method, **measurements with units/scales and timing**, and a limitation.

## Consent & Privacy

- **Consent** = a meaningful chance to understand what participation involves and to say no. One "Accept all" click isn't informed consent for every later use.
- **Purpose shift:** using data for a different purpose than people expected (site analytics → targeted housing ads) raises the privacy risk
- **"Anonymous" isn't unidentifiable:** browsing patterns + IP address + device details, or a wearable device's daily routine, can act as a fingerprint

## Writing Unbiased Survey Questions

| Problem | Example | Fix |
|:---------------|:------------------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Leading / loaded** | "Don't you agree the *overpriced* dining..." | Neutral wording, no opinion words |
| **Double-barreled** | Asks about affordability *and* eating well in one question | One concept per question |
| **Vague** | "Do you get *enough* sleep?" | Ask for a number, with units |
| **No time frame** | "How often do you..." | "During the past 7 days..." |
| **Missing options** | Only "car" or "bus" for commuting | Exhaustive options, "select all", "Other" |
| **Overlapping bins** | 1–2 hrs, 2–3 hrs | Non-overlapping: 1–2, 3–4 |
| **Measures the wrong thing** | "How much does social media *harm* you?" when the goal is time spent | Measure the predictor and outcome separately |
